summary: Defines a portion of the Management Information Base for managing Traffic Engineered (TE) tunnels, such as MPLS label switched paths.

eli5.summary: It is a list of dials and gauges that let a network operator watch and control the special routes set up for certain traffic.

subtitle: SNMP objects for configuring and monitoring traffic-engineered tunnels such as MPLS label switched paths.

tldr.problem: Operators need a standard way to configure traffic-engineered (TE) tunnels, assign paths to them and watch how they behave, instead of using vendor-specific tools.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the TE-MIB module, an SMIv2 module with general TE information, a tunnel table, a path table and a hop table, plus four notifications and compliance statements.
tldr.outcome: A tunnel can be built row by row through SNMP at its ingress router, which then signals the rest of the path with a protocol such as RSVP-TE. The RFC has been updated by RFC 9141.

facts.label: Notification rate limit
facts.value: At most one per minute each

today: RFC 3970 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 9141. The RFC itself notes that the module covers configuring and monitoring a tunnel only at its ingress.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 3970 defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing Traffic Engineered (TE) Tunnels, for example Multi-Protocol Label Switched Paths. The module lets an operator configure TE Tunnels, assign one or more paths to a tunnel, and monitor operational aspects such as the number of octets and packets that have passed through it.

As written, the module can only configure or monitor a tunnel at its ingress. The ingress is then expected to use a protocol such as RSVP-TE to signal the other routers on the path. Extending the module to other points of a tunnel is left for further study.

The module is written for the Internet-Standard Management Framework. Objects are normally accessed through SNMP and defined with SMIv2, as described in STD 58.
sections.eli5: The dials only control the start of the route. The first router then tells the other routers along the way what to do.

sections.title: Four Parts of the MIB Module
sections.content:
The module has four parts: general Traffic Engineering information, a table of tunnels, a table of paths and a table of hops. The first part reports the link state protocols that carry TE information, the signaling protocols that set up tunnels, how many tunnels are configured and operational, and a mapping of Administrative Group numbers (called Resource Classes in RFC 2702) to names.

A tunnel is a logical entity. Its instantiation is one or more paths, and each path has a route, or sequence of hops. A path has a dual index: the tunnel it belongs to first, then the path itself. Tunnel rows record the name, endpoints, current state (up or down), octet and packet counts, how long the tunnel has been up and how many state transitions it has had.

A hop can be loose, meaning the path eventually traverses the node, or strict, meaning the node (and possibly the link) must be next. A hop can be an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address, an Autonomous System number or an unnumbered interface index. The hop table has one index for a list of hops and a second for each hop in order, so the recorded route of a path is read from tePathRecordedRoute using indexes 1, 2, and so on.
sections.eli5: Think of a road trip plan. A tunnel is the trip, a path is one way to drive it, and hops are the towns you pass through, in order.

sections.title: Objects in the Path and Tunnel Tables
sections.content:
Beyond names and endpoints, each path row carries the constraints for a route. tePathType says whether a path is primary, standby or secondary. tePathBandwidth is the configured bandwidth in thousands of bits per second. Three bit vectors, tePathIncludeAny, tePathIncludeAll and tePathExclude, constrain which links a path may use by their administrative groups. Group numbers run from 1 to 32, and group n is bit n-1.

Setup and hold priorities are integers from 0 to 7, where 0 is the highest priority and 7 the lowest. The defaults are 7 for setup and 0 for hold. tePathProperties is a bit map of recordRoute, cspf, makeBeforeBreak, mergeable, fastReroute and protected.

Each path also reports its operational status, its computed route (the route calculated to satisfy the constraints) and its recorded route (the actual path as recorded by the signaling protocol). Tunnel names must be unique, and a set that reuses a name must return an inconsistentValue error. The tunnel state is one of unknown, up, down or testing.
sections.eli5: Each route has a list of rules, like "only use roads with these labels" and "go around roads with those labels". There is also a priority from 0 to 7, where 0 wins.

sections.title: Creating, Changing and Deleting a Tunnel
sections.content:
To create a tunnel, a manager reads teNextTunnelIndex to obtain a free index and creates the row, with all parameters, as createAndGo or createAndWait. Paths are then created the same way using teTunnelNextPathIndex. A path is computed and signaled when both the path and its enclosing tunnel have RowStatus active.

To build a configured route, the manager gets a free hop index from teNextPathHopIndex, adds hops one by one using the secondary index, setting the address type, address and hop type for each, and finally sets tePathConfiguredRoute to that hop index.

The index objects work as a simple lock. Two managers may read the same value, but only the first SET succeeds because the agent checks that the value is still unused. The other manager must re-read the object for a new value. A value of 0 means no more rows can be created.

Changing some properties may require setting RowStatus to notInService and back to active, which re-signals the paths. Setting a tunnel's RowStatus to destroy deletes it and all its paths, and a single path can be destroyed the same way.
sections.eli5: To make a new route, you first take a numbered ticket so nobody else uses your number. Then you fill in the form, one town at a time, and switch the route on when it is ready.

sections.title: Relation to Interface and Tunnel MIBs
sections.content:
A TE tunnel can extend two other MIB modules: the Interfaces MIB and the IP Tunnel MIB. To do so, the tunnel index teTunnelIndex is assigned a valid ifIndex from the interface table. If a tunnel is treated as an interface, a new interface row is created first, and the tunnel row uses the same number.

Only a tunnel that is an interface may also be an IP tunnel, and only if its encapsulation is IP. In that case its ifType should be set to tunnel(131). A tunnel that is not an interface SHOULD use a teTunnelIndex of at least 2^24, so that it cannot clash with ordinary interface numbers.
sections.eli5: If a tunnel is also treated like a network plug, it uses the plug's number. If not, it takes a very big number so it never gets mixed up with real plugs.

sections.title: Notifications and Compliance
sections.content:
Four notifications can be sent, but only if teNotificationEnable is true; it defaults to false. teTunnelUp and teTunnelDown fire when a tunnel changes state. A tunnel is up when at least one of its paths is up. teTunnelChanged fires when the active path changes or a new path becomes active. teTunnelRerouted fires when the active path stays the same but its route changes. Each MUST be limited to at most one every minute, in case the tunnel flaps.

For compliance, all objects are mandatory. For minimal compliance, all objects MAY be implemented read-only. For full compliance, all objects must be implemented to their stated MAX-ACCESS. Notifications are optional.
sections.eli5: The tunnel can ring a bell when it goes up, goes down or changes route. To avoid a noisy bell, it rings at most once a minute.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC warns that unauthorized changes to the admin group, tunnel, path or path hop tables may cause tunnel flapping, changed tunnel paths or disrupted traffic. Unauthorized readers could trace traffic patterns, traffic volumes and tunnel paths, which some providers consider proprietary and confidential.

It lists the sensitive tables. The admin group table changes the meaning of include and exclude constraints, so traffic could take unintended routes. The tunnel table affects many tunnel properties, the path table affects constraints and path status, and the hop table affects the route followed.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC RECOMMENDS the SNMPv3 security features, including authentication and privacy, and says deploying older SNMP versions is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators remain responsible for configuring access properly.
sections.eli5: If a stranger could turn the dials, they could send traffic down the wrong roads. So only trusted people should be allowed to read or change them.
